newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House Budget chair says wedded to CBO numbers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House Budget chair says wedded to CBO numbers.

text.p: House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich said Tuesday that he was fixed on using the more conservative Congressional Budget Office economic estimates over White House estimates for budget purposes.
The Republican from Ohio, asked after a hearing whether he was wedded to the CBO estimates, replied: "I'm wedded to conservative economics ... the answer is yes."
CBO is analyzing the president's budget and is expected to reveal some of its early analysis at a congressional hearing Thursday when the agency's director testifies.
The House Budget Committee's analysis of Clinton's budget said that using CBO deficit projections, the president's proposal would have a $36.5 billion deficit in fiscal 2002.
Clinton's proposal expects a $17 billion surplus in 2002.
Kasich said he believed there would be a budget agreement this year. "I think we'll get something and then we have to come back next year, and the next year," he said.
He said he saw no reason for the Republicans not to have their own budget proposal, rather than just work from Clinton's plan.
"I just really do not see a reason why the Republicans do not develop their own proposal," he said, adding that he had not spoken to House Speaker Newt Gingrich about it yet.
Gingrich and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Republican from Mississippi, earlier Tuesday left the door open for developing a bipartisan budget proposal with the Clinton administration.

"My sense is that it's very hard to negotiate unless you know where you are," Kasich said. "We have not resolved our major differences on the economics. When you take their proposals and put them in with the CBO economic assumptions, we don't really have much change in the deficits," he said.

White House Office of Management and Budget Director Franklin Raines said at the House Budget Committee hearing that the differences between the economic estimates of CBO and his office were "remarkably small."

The OMB economic assumptions should guide policy making because it has been slightly better at estimating the deficit than CBO in recent years, Raines said. "Both of us have greatly underestimated the performance of the economy," he added, referring to the recent track record.
If there were a plan to balance the budget today, Raines said he believed "we will exceed our estimates again as we have in the past four years."
